title: Follow the Order: What Happens Between “Buy” and “Delivered”
basis: Reconstructed from the published chapter (posts/01-journey-of-an-order/index.md) and its former spec.md, whose Non-goals, Open questions, Decision log, Sources and Changelog are carried over. One spec paragraph per unit of the published chapter, in its order. It is a contract, not a description: the places where the published chapter does not yet do what the spec asks are listed under open_questions.

know: The thirteen steps of an order and the system that holds the order at each one.
The three status lines of an order: money, goods and returns.
believe: An order is a chain of promises, and it breaks at the handoffs between systems, rarely inside one.
can_do: Given a late, lost, duplicated or misread order, name the handoff at which it went wrong.

audience.who: Readers new to commerce architecture in their first weeks at a merchant, a vendor or an agency; most of all the engineer or product manager who has been handed 'the order flow' without a map, and anyone who answers 'where is my order' for a living.
already_knows: What buying something online is like from the shopper's side.
Roughly what an API, a database and a queue are.
Kestrel & Pine and its 2026 incidents, in outline (meet-kestrel-and-pine).
The names of the sixteen failure patterns (where-commerce-platforms-go-wrong).
does_not_know: Promise, handoff, entity, fulfillment order, status line, idempotency, reconciliation, system of record.
SKU, PSP, ERP, WMS, iPaaS, 3PL, SaaS, EDI, VAT, IFRS, webhook, theme, marketplace connector.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a description of an order that support cannot explain, the reader names the handoff and the two systems on either side of it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: An order shows 'Delivered' in the shop and 'In picking' in the warehouse. Using only this chapter: which handoff would you inspect first, and why?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The goods status line between warehouse and storefront; the reader separates it from the money and returns lines.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every term the rest of Part I relies on (handoff, promise, status line, system) is defined here before it is used.
Given a refund that went out twice, the reader names which of the four message failures it is and the two capabilities that contain it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A customer returned a jacket and was refunded twice. Using only this chapter: what kind of failure is this, and what two things would a merchant need to be able to do to catch it and stop it happening again?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A duplicated message (two senders, no shared record of what was done). Compare two systems' copies (reconciliation) to detect it; make a repeated message have no second effect (idempotency) so it is safe.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (callouts and paragraphs p01 to p04) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Different views of one order; the steps and the vocabulary of promises and handoffs; status lines; one order followed system by system; how handoffs fail and how failures are caught; vendor documentation and law as evidence.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

thesis.question: What has to happen, in which systems, for one online order to be found, bought, paid, shipped, delivered, returned and accounted for?
thesis.claim: For one order to be found, bought, paid, shipped, delivered, returned and accounted for, thirteen steps must each complete in a system that keeps its own copy of the order and learns of changes only by message; the order is therefore a chain of promises between systems, and a break in that chain is a message that arrived late, was lost, was duplicated or was misread.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that an order is one record with one status, and that failures are bugs inside the system that holds it.
thesis.so_what: If failures live in handoffs, a merchant looks for them between systems and gives each handoff an owner, instead of replacing the system that reported the symptom.
thesis.how_why: Each system holds its own copy of the order and learns of changes only by message; money, goods and returns move through separate states, so one status word cannot be true in every system at once.

supporting_claims.claim: Each team sees only the part of an order its own system holds, and nobody owns the path between the systems.
The journey has the same thirteen steps for every order, and its promises are made early by one system and kept late by another.
Every handoff is a message with requirements (freshness, consistency, speed, availability) that someone has to set.
Money, goods and returns move through separate status lines, so one status word cannot be true in every system at once.
A single order becomes several copies in several systems, each correct about its own part.
A message fails in only four ways (late, lost, duplicated, misread), and comparison and safe resending contain all four.

role.contribution: Supplies the journey and the vocabulary (promise, handoff, status line) that every later chapter places itself on.

additional_patterns.applies_to: evas-jacket and in-practice: both follow the order of the journey's steps
joins: four failure modes in the same shape

flow.rationale: The scene poses the problem (no shared map) and names the systems, so that no later section uses one the reader has not met; the steps, the two words, the entities and the status lines are the vocabulary the walk needs, in that order: the steps table shows promises made and kept, so the two words are defined directly after it; the entities come next because a handoff is a message about them; and the status lines come last because they need the difference between an order and a shipment. The walk supplies the arrows the failure analysis points at; the failure analysis opens with the four ways a message fails, one incident each, and then states the requirements each handoff must meet, which the incidents have just shown being missed; the two failure sections sit together, the four modes first and the per-step table second, because the table applies the modes and their two remedies and would repeat them if it stood apart; public evidence, gathered in one section and not spread through the earlier ones, comes after the reader has seen the handoffs and how they fail, because before that its warnings about repeated and out-of-order messages would answer a question the reader has not yet asked; the scale stages come last because they add no new idea, only more of the same handoffs, and before the failure sections the reader could not say what multiplies. Putting the walk first would stop every sentence for a definition; putting the failure analysis first would name incidents on arrows the reader has not yet seen. One incident, the Three-Status Order, is told before the walk on purpose: it is the evidence that one status word fails, it needs only the systems named in the scene and the difference between an order and a shipment, and the failure analysis later refers back to it in a line instead of retelling it.

hook.content: After a shopper pays, the warehouse sees a pick list, finance an invoice and support a service ticket. When those records disagree, the shopper waits while every team believes its part is complete.

bridge.from_reader_world: Anyone who has waited for a parcel, or been asked where one is, knows an order from the outside as one thing with one status.
bridge.to_topic: Inside the merchant it is thirteen steps across several systems, joined by handoffs that each have to carry a promise another system can keep.

thesis_statement.text: An order is thirteen steps, each completed in a system that keeps its own copy and learns of changes only by message: a chain of promises between systems, in which a break is a message that arrived late, was lost, was duplicated or was misread.
thesis_statement.placement: KEY POINTS callout, first and second bullets, and paragraph p02

roadmap.placement: IN THIS CHAPTER callout and paragraph p03

promises.promise: Start from four colleagues' four drawings of one order.
Name what an order needs: its steps, the words promise and handoff, the things it is made of, and its three status lines.
Follow one order through the systems that hold those records.
Show the four ways the messages between systems fail, the failure to expect at each step, and the checks that let a merchant explain what happened.
Confirm the account against what vendors and the law document, and show what changes as a merchant grows.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: After a shopper pays, the warehouse, finance and support each work from a different record of the same order, and when the records disagree the shopper waits while every team believes its part is done.

evidence.what: A pick list, an invoice and a service ticket for one order.
evidence.shows: The reader can picture three honest records that do not add up to one answer.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An order passes through thirteen steps and several systems, and each handoff between them must carry a promise another system can keep.

transition_in.carries_over: The teams and their separate records.
transition_in.introduces: The steps and handoffs that connect them, and the promise each handoff carries.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The chapter starts from four drawings of one order, names what an order needs (its steps, the words promise and handoff, its entities, its three status lines), follows one order through the systems that hold it, shows how the messages between them fail and the checks that explain what happened, sets that against what vendors and the law document, and ends with what changes as a merchant grows.

transition_in.introduces: The order in which the chapter takes them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The order followed throughout is Eva Janssen's jacket and socks from Kestrel & Pine, from search to delivery and return.

transition_in.introduces: The one order used to show it.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: Four Drawings of One Order
sections.controlling_idea: Four colleagues drew four correct pictures of one order, each centred on their own system, and nobody drew the path between the boxes because nobody owned it.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the chapter's problem before any vocabulary: the absence of a shared map, not a failure of any one system.

flow.rationale: The request, the four drawings, what they share, the systems the drawings contain, then the response: the reader reaches the gap between the boxes the way Noor did and knows the boxes by name before any later section uses them.

transition_in.carries_over: The introduction's teams with their separate records.
transition_in.introduces: One company where four people were asked to draw the whole order.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In January 2027 the new head of engineering asked four colleagues to draw what happens to an online order.
The storefront owner put the commerce platform at the centre and the head of operations put the warehouse system there.

evidence.what: Milan Petrov's drawing centred on the platform; Daniel Okafor's on Duiven's warehouse system.
evidence.shows: Each centre is the system its author runs.

transition_in.carries_over: The request to draw the order.
transition_in.introduces: The first two drawings.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The finance director centred the ERP, the system that keeps the books and the stock ledger; the integration engineer drew thirty-four boxes and ran out of time; and each had drawn the part they could see.

evidence.what: Sanne de Wit's drawing centred on the ERP; Ruben Alves's thirty-four boxes.
evidence.shows: Even the person who sees every integration cannot draw the whole in twenty minutes.

transition_in.introduces: Two more, and what all four have in common.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: None of the four drawings was wrong; what nobody had drawn, because nobody owned it, was the order's path between the boxes.

evidence.what: Figure of the four drawings.
evidence.shows: The gap between the boxes is visible when the four are set side by side.

transition_in.introduces: What is missing from all of them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The boxes in the four drawings come down to seven systems on the order's path, a system being any software or outside company's service that takes part in handling an order; the company runs more, and a few appear in the failure stories. Six keep their own record of the order or of their part of it (the shop platform, the payment provider, the warehouse system, the ERP, the carrier and the returns portal), and the seventh, the integration platform, carries the messages between them and keeps none.

evidence.what: Kestrel & Pine's systems, each with a one-clause gloss of what it does: platform (takes the order), payment provider (collects the money), warehouse management system (picks and ships), ERP (books and stock ledger), carrier (delivers and reports tracking), returns portal (accepts return requests), integration platform (iPaaS, carries messages).
evidence.shows: The reader has a fixed cast for the walk, and is told that other systems exist, so the marketplace connector and an agency script in the failure stories are not a surprise.

transition_in.carries_over: The boxes of the four drawings and the undrawn path between them.
transition_in.introduces: What the boxes are: the seven systems, named once for the whole chapter.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The response was to follow one order through every system, and before doing that the reader needs the thirteen steps, the two words for how an order moves, the things it is made of, and the reason it has three status lines and not one.

transition_in.carries_over: The seven systems and the undrawn path between them.
transition_in.introduces: The method that draws the path, and the vocabulary it needs first.

sections.heading: The Journey in Thirteen Steps
sections.controlling_idea: Every consumer order passes through roughly the same thirteen steps, in which promises are made early by one system and kept late by another.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the journey its fixed shape and puts the made-early, kept-late pattern in front of the reader as a table.

transition_in.carries_over: The need for the steps before the walk.
transition_in.introduces: The steps themselves.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The steps are the same on every platform, and each one carries a promise, a statement to the customer that some system later has to make true.

evidence.what: Thirteen steps: what happens, the promise made, who usually has to keep it.
evidence.shows: Reading across a row shows that the promise-maker and the promise-keeper differ.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three things in the table matter before any technology: promises are made in minutes and kept over days, the system that makes a promise is rarely the one that keeps it, and the return and accounting steps are routine, not exceptions.

evidence.what: 24% of items Kestrel & Pine sold online in 2026 came back, and every order became an invoice.
evidence.shows: The late steps are routine, not exceptions.

transition_in.introduces: The three patterns in it that the rest of the chapter depends on.

sections.heading: Promises and Handoffs
sections.controlling_idea: A promise is a statement to the customer that some system must later make true, and a handoff is the accepted message by which responsibility for the order passes from one system to the next.

advances_thesis.how: Defines the two words the thesis is stated in; the requirements a handoff carries follow once the walk has shown the handoffs.

flow.rationale: Promise first, because a handoff is defined as what carries a promise to the system that must keep it.

transition_in.carries_over: The table's two columns: the promise made at each step and who has to keep it.
transition_in.introduces: The two words those columns rest on, promise and handoff, defined.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The table and the introduction have already used two words for the pairing, promise and handoff, and this section defines them because they carry the book's argument.

Because a promise is made in one system and kept in others, a commerce platform in this book's sense is the whole set of systems that make and keep promises; the shop platform, the product that takes the order, is one of them.

evidence.what: 'In stock', '€199', 'ordered before 22:00, delivered tomorrow', 'free returns within 14 days'.
evidence.shows: Each is made in one system and can only be made true in another.

transition_in.introduces: The first word, promise, already defined with the steps table: here its examples and what it implies for the word platform, without defining it a second time.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A handoff is the moment responsibility passes from one system to another; it is always carried by a message, and it is complete only when the receiver has accepted that message.

evidence.what: 'Charge €235', 'paid', 'pick these three lines'; API call, file, webhook, queue entry, EDI document; figure of the journey as handoffs.
evidence.shows: Each handoff can be named as one message with a sender and a receiver.

transition_in.introduces: The second word: how the order reaches the system that must keep the promise.

sections.heading: The Things an Order Is Made Of
sections.controlling_idea: Commerce systems keep records of a small set of entities, and a cart, an order and a shipment are three different ones.

advances_thesis.how: Names the records the systems hold, so that the walk can say which system holds which.

transition_in.carries_over: Handoffs as messages that pass responsibility for the order.
transition_in.introduces: What those messages are about: the things an order is made of.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The entities of commerce are the nouns every platform keeps records of, under its own names.

evidence.what: The entities of an order and what each one is.
evidence.shows: The reader gets one plain definition per noun before any system uses it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A cart is a draft and not an order, and an order is not a shipment: the fulfillment order is the warehouse's unit of work in between.

evidence.what: 70.22% average cart abandonment across fifty studies published 2006 to 2025.
evidence.shows: Most carts never become orders, so the two cannot be the same record.

transition_in.introduces: The two pairs newcomers merge.

sections.heading: One Order, Three Status Lines
sections.controlling_idea: An order's money, goods and returns move through separate states, so reducing them to one status word makes systems disagree.

advances_thesis.how: Removes the newcomer's assumption that an order has one status, which the walk and the failure analysis both depend on.

flow.rationale: The claim, its plain-words reading with the goods line drawn, then the incident: the reader meets the incident already knowing what the lines are. The vendors' versions of the same lines are gathered with the other public evidence in 'In Practice'.

transition_in.carries_over: The entities, and the difference between an order and a shipment.
transition_in.introduces: The reason one status word cannot describe an order made of several things that move separately.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: One status per order does not work, because the money, the goods and the return move independently; each moves through its own sequence of states, a status line, and an order has three.
Combinations such as paid and not shipped, or returned and not yet refunded, are normal states, not errors.

evidence.what: The goods status line for a simple order.
evidence.shows: One line has its own states and transitions, independent of money.

transition_in.carries_over: The claim that an order has three status lines.
transition_in.introduces: What that means in plain words, and the goods line on its own.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine's Three-Status Order shows the cost: an integration that could not represent a partial shipment marked the whole order fulfilled when the first parcel left.

evidence.what: Order #1052877: fleece shipped 7 December 2026, socks waited a week; platform showed Delivered after the carrier's scan.
evidence.shows: Flattening the goods line produced a status that was false for half the order.

transition_in.carries_over: Separate status lines as the norm.
transition_in.introduces: One order where they were flattened into one.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Each system's status described part of the order, and nobody could give the customer the useful answer, that the order ships in two parcels.

evidence.what: WMS In picking until the socks shipped; ERP waiting for 'order complete'; eleven support tickets.
evidence.shows: Three partial truths with no owner of the combined view.

transition_in.introduces: What the other systems showed and what the customer was left without.

sections.heading: Eva's Jacket, System by System
sections.controlling_idea: Followed step by step, one order ends up as several copies in several systems, each correct about its own part.

advances_thesis.how: Performs the walk the scene called for, so every later claim about handoffs can point at a named arrow.

flow.rationale: The order as placed, then the thirteen steps in the sequence they happened, one or two numbered steps per paragraph, so the reader can match each paragraph to rows of the thirteen-step table; the per-system table and its question come only after the last step. Accounting (step 13) starts at dispatch and is told last, with the date said.

transition_in.carries_over: The steps, promises, handoffs, entities and status lines.
transition_in.introduces: One order followed through all of them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The walk uses one fictional order whose numbers are fixed for the whole book.
On Tuesday 13 April 2027 at 21:14, Eva orders a €199 jacket and two €18 pairs of socks, pays €235 by iDEAL, and is promised delivery the next day.

evidence.what: Order #1072455; free shipping over €75; 22:00 cut-off; figure of the order across systems.
evidence.shows: Every later step refers to these figures.

transition_in.introduces: The order itself and the promise it carries.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Steps 1 and 2: the product page's price, stock and delivery promise each came from a different source, the stock figure up to an hour and a quarter old.

evidence.what: Price from the platform's price list; stock from the platform's inventory field fed by the ERP and the WMS; delivery promise from a static rule in the theme.
evidence.shows: Three promises on one page rest on three sources of different age.

transition_in.introduces: Where the promises on the product page came from.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Steps 3 and 4: at checkout the platform calls pricing, promotions, tax, availability, shipping rates and the payment provider within seconds and turns the answers into one total.

evidence.what: The jacket and two pairs of socks, free shipping, €235 including 21% Dutch VAT, several payment methods offered.
evidence.shows: Checkout is an orchestration of other systems' answers.

transition_in.introduces: The checkout that fixes them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Step 5: the payment provider collects the money and tells the platform by a webhook, a message it pushes when the payment changes state.

evidence.what: iDEAL as an instant charge, captured automatically, with no chargeback and a 15-minute session timeout.
evidence.shows: The payment result arrives as a separate message, not as part of the checkout call.

transition_in.introduces: How the money is taken and how the platform learns of it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Step 6: the platform creates the order with payment pending a moment before the result arrives, commits stock from its own figure, and publishes an order event; the order now exists in one system.

evidence.what: Order created pending, then marked paid; confirmation e-mail; event to the iPaaS.
evidence.shows: Steps 5 and 6 overlap, which is why the order must tolerate a late payment message.

transition_in.introduces: The order record it marks as paid.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Step 7: the integration platform creates a fulfillment order in the warehouse system, which picks, packs and reports the shipment back to the platform and the ERP.

evidence.what: Picked in a morning wave on Wednesday 14 April, one box, tracking number returned through the iPaaS.
evidence.shows: The warehouse's record is a different object created by a message.

transition_in.introduces: Its first copy in a second.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Steps 8 and 9: the carrier delivers on Thursday, a day later than promised, because the storefront's delivery promise is static: a fixed cut-off rule that dates from a previous warehouse and does not ask the current one.

evidence.what: PostNL collected Wednesday evening, delivered Thursday 15 April; the 'before 22:00' rule dates from the third-party warehouse in Tiel.
evidence.shows: A promise made from a static rule was broken with every system working as designed.

transition_in.introduces: Its delivery, and the promise it broke.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Step 10: a service agent asked about the order would have worked from five separate screens.

evidence.what: 'The five tabs': platform order screen, WMS, shipping tracking page, PSP console, returns portal; ERP visible only to finance.
evidence.shows: No single place holds the order's whole state.

transition_in.introduces: What service could have seen during it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Step 11: the returns portal, a separate product, accepts an exchange request and in doing so makes two promises on the merchant's behalf.

evidence.what: Exchange for size L requested Monday 19 April; PostNL return label issued; platform told to expect a return and an exchange for size L.
evidence.shows: A fifth system now makes promises others must keep.

evidence.what: A consumer may withdraw within 14 days of receiving the goods.
evidence.shows: One of the two promises is fixed by law, not by the merchant.

transition_in.introduces: The return, which starts in yet another system.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Step 12: the warehouse receives and grades the return, the platform closes it, and the exchange order for size L ships the same day.

evidence.what: Received at Duiven 22 April, graded resellable; refund variant: €199 by iDEAL reversal and a credit note.
evidence.shows: The return is a second journey through the same systems in reverse.

transition_in.introduces: The goods coming back and the replacement going out.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Step 13: the ERP invoices the order on dispatch, matches the payout (the provider's transfer of the collected money to the merchant), and records the exchange as a credit note and a new invoice.

evidence.what: €235 gross: €194.21 net and €40.79 VAT at 21%; credit note for size M and new invoice for size L, netting to zero.
evidence.shows: Finance holds its own version of the order, with its own timing.

evidence.what: Revenue is recognized when the goods are delivered, not when the customer pays.
evidence.shows: Finance's clock differs from the storefront's by rule.

transition_in.introduces: What finance records for all of it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Set side by side, what each system that held the order knew at each moment (the carrier, which knew only the parcel, left out) explains why the four colleagues drew four pictures.

evidence.what: What each system knew at each moment of the order.
evidence.shows: A column is one system's world; a row is the disagreement between them.

transition_in.carries_over: The thirteen steps of the walk.
transition_in.introduces: The same walk read per system.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Each system holds its own copy of the order, or of its part, each correct about that part, and the open question is which copy to believe when two disagree.

transition_in.carries_over: The table of what each system knew.
transition_in.introduces: The question it leaves, which another chapter answers.

sections.heading: Why the Joins Are Where Things Break
sections.controlling_idea: A message between systems can fail in only four ways (late, lost, duplicated, misread), all four have happened at Kestrel & Pine, and each failure missed a requirement the business had set for that handoff.

advances_thesis.how: Turns the walk's arrows into the chapter's main claim about where failures live.

flow.rationale: The four failure modes first, in the same shape, one incident each, because they are the simple part and their incidents are then known when the requirements table names them; then the requirements each handoff must meet, which the incidents showed being missed; then the remedies that cover all four.

transition_in.carries_over: Copies of the order in several systems, joined by messages.
transition_in.introduces: The ways those messages fail.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Every arrow in the walk is a message, as is every arrow like it elsewhere in the company, and a message can go wrong in only four ways, all of which have happened at Kestrel & Pine.

Late: the stock figure that was up to an hour and a quarter old on Eva's product page took one more hop to reach the marketplaces, the other channels that sell the same stock, and that let them sell a sold-out jacket for up to two hours.

evidence.what: Black Friday 2026: sold out at 19:40; 1,340 units oversold, 1,120 orders cancelled or delayed, about €96,000; order queue to the WMS backed up four hours.
evidence.shows: Lateness alone, with every system up, produced the company's largest loss.

transition_in.introduces: The first.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Lost: when the marketplace connector retired a version of its interface that a script still used, a stock update stopped being sent, and a message that is not sent produces no error.

evidence.what: February 2027: the marketplace connector kept sending bol its last figures for two days.
evidence.shows: The receiver cannot tell silence from 'no change'.

transition_in.introduces: The second way.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Duplicated: at the return step that Eva's exchange passed through, two senders refunded the same returns, with no shared record of what had already been done.

evidence.what: January 2027: 212 returns refunded twice, €19,400, most recovered.
evidence.shows: A second, well-meant message did the damage.

transition_in.introduces: The third way.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Misread: the Three-Status Order, recalled in a line and not retold, was three systems reading the same two-parcel order differently.

evidence.what: 'Shipped' meant 'all shipped' to one system and 'first parcel shipped' to another; figure of the four failures.
evidence.shows: The message arrived once and on time and still produced a wrong state.

transition_in.introduces: The fourth way.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Each of those failures missed a requirement the business sets for a handoff, usually without writing it down: how fresh, how consistent, how fast, and what happens when the receiver is down.

evidence.what: Freshness, consistency, speed and availability targets for the main handoffs of a consumer order; targets illustrative.
evidence.shows: The requirements can be written per handoff in one line each; every merchant has these rows, written down or not.

transition_in.carries_over: The four failures, each at one handoff of the walk.
transition_in.introduces: The requirements each handoff must meet, which those failures missed.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The field's answer is two ideas: idempotency, so a repeated message has no second effect whoever sends it, and reconciliation, so two systems' copies are compared and the late, the lost and the misread show up as differences.

evidence.what: The first weekly stock reconciliation, May 2027: 2.3% of active variants differed between the WMS and the shop platform.
evidence.shows: A comparison of two copies finds differences no error message reported.

transition_in.carries_over: The four ways a message fails and the requirements they miss.
transition_in.introduces: The two ideas that contain them.

sections.heading: When It Goes Wrong at Each Step
sections.controlling_idea: Every stretch of the journey has an ordinary failure, and most are detected by comparing two systems' copies and recovered by sending a message again safely; the rest are caught by a check at the point of work.

advances_thesis.how: Extends the four failure modes along the whole journey, with the detection and the recovery for each, and says how far the two remedies reach.

transition_in.carries_over: The four ways a message fails, and idempotency and reconciliation as the two remedies.
transition_in.introduces: The failure to expect at each of the thirteen steps, with how it is detected and recovered.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Each stretch of the journey has an ordinary failure, and none needs a disaster: each happens in a normal week.

evidence.what: Per step: what goes wrong, how it is detected, how it is recovered.
evidence.shows: Each step has a failure that can be named in advance.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Most detections in the table are reconciliations and most recoveries are safe resends; the rest are checks at the point of work, such as scanning at the packing bench, so a merchant that can compare and safely resend is most of the way to a reliable journey.

sections.heading: In Practice: What the Public Record Says
sections.controlling_idea: Vendor documentation and regulation describe the journey's handoffs precisely: each is a message that can be delayed or repeated, responsibility passes only when the receiver accepts it, and the order's three status lines are kept apart; the chapter's vendor evidence is gathered here.

advances_thesis.how: Shows that the chapter's account is what payment providers, platforms and the law themselves document, not the author's construction.

flow.rationale: The evidence follows the journey's own order: payment, warehouse, the order record's status families (whose 'fulfilled' is not 'delivered'), the carrier's tracking, the law's deadlines, the books.

transition_in.introduces: What real vendors and the law say about the same handoffs.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Vendor documentation and regulation describe the journey's steps with precision, and this section gathers that public record in the journey's order.

The vendors confirm what the walk showed, that the payment result reaches the shop as a separate message, and add that the message may arrive more than once (duplicated) or after a newer one (late); the same providers document the payment details the walk relied on and the idempotency key.

evidence.what: Stripe's checkout guide warns against relying on the landing page; commercetools creates the order with payment pending.
evidence.shows: Two vendors document that the result arrives separately from the shopper.
evidence.source: Stripe and commercetools documentation, n.d., accessed November 2026

evidence.what: Retries 'for up to three days'; 'doesn't guarantee the delivery of events in the order that they're generated'; endpoints 'might occasionally receive the same event more than once'.
evidence.shows: Duplication and reordering are stated properties of the handoff.
evidence.source: Stripe webhook documentation, n.d., accessed November 2026

evidence.what: Mollie's webhook carries only a payment identifier and no status.
evidence.shows: The receiver must fetch the state itself, so a forged call cannot mark an order paid.

evidence.what: iDEAL as an instant charge, captured automatically, with no chargeback and a 15-minute session timeout.
evidence.shows: The walk's step 5 rests on the provider's own description.

evidence.what: A client sends an idempotency key with each request, and a retry with the same key returns the saved result.
evidence.shows: The mechanism is documented and in production at a payment provider.

transition_in.introduces: Its first case: the payment handoff.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The vendors confirm that a handoff needs acceptance: a warehouse must accept an order before it is responsible for it, after acceptance a cancellation needs its agreement, and since the warehouse may also refuse, a refusal is an answer within the handoff, not a fifth way for a message to fail.

evidence.what: A fulfillment request that the warehouse service accepts or rejects; fulfillment cannot be created before acceptance.
evidence.shows: The handoff is a two-way exchange that settles who controls the next step.
evidence.source: Shopify fulfillment-service documentation, n.d., accessed November 2026

transition_in.carries_over: The payment handoff, where the receiver must be ready for a repeated message.
transition_in.introduces: The warehouse handoff, where the receiver must accept the message before it is responsible.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The major shop platforms keep separate status families on one order, which match the book's money, goods and returns lines, and neither's 'fulfilled' means delivered.

evidence.what: Shopify: order, payment and fulfillment status families. commercetools: OrderState, PaymentState, ShipmentState and per-item return states.
evidence.shows: Two independent vendors separate the same three lines, and neither's 'fulfilled' means delivered.
evidence.source: Shopify and commercetools documentation, n.d., accessed November 2026

transition_in.carries_over: The warehouse handoff and its fulfillment.
transition_in.introduces: How two shop platform vendors record the order's status lines that these handoffs move.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Tracking events are the customer's view of the journey, and without them the merchant cannot answer where the order is.

evidence.what: 'If you fulfill an order without a tracking number, then no shipping updates are received.'
evidence.shows: The delivered status depends on a third party's messages.
evidence.source: Shopify order-status documentation, n.d., accessed November 2026

evidence.what: 'Where is my order' requests were about 18% of incoming support contacts in one helpdesk vendor's customer base.
evidence.shows: The cost of a missing view falls on service.
evidence.source: Gorgias, article updated November 2023; one vendor's data

transition_in.introduces: The carrier's messages back.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The law fixes the outer bounds of three promises: delivery, withdrawal and refund.

evidence.what: Delivery 'not later than 30 days from the conclusion of the contract'; 14 days to withdraw; reimbursement 'not later than 14 days'.
evidence.shows: Three of the journey's promises have legal deadlines the systems must be able to meet.

transition_in.introduces: What the law requires.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A return is recorded as a new linked document, never as an edit of the original invoice.

evidence.what: An invoice is numbered on confirmation and then locked; a credit note is the legal way to cancel or adjust it.
evidence.shows: Finance's record is append-only, which is why an exchange produces two new documents.
evidence.source: Odoo accounting documentation, version 18, accessed November 2026

sections.heading: Across Scale Stages
sections.controlling_idea: The thirteen steps stay the same as a merchant grows; what grows is the number of systems, channels and stock locations between them.

advances_thesis.how: Explains why the same journey breaks more often as the business grows: the handoffs multiply.

transition_in.carries_over: The journey and its handoffs as documented for any merchant.
transition_in.introduces: How the number of handoffs changes over a merchant's four stages.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Across the four stages (starting, growing, omnichannel, group) the steps are unchanged and the number of systems, channels and locations holding copies increases.

evidence.what: Kestrel & Pine in 2016 to 2018 as one hosted platform with an outside payment provider, warehouse and carrier.
evidence.shows: The starting stage has few handoffs to own.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine reached the third stage, omnichannel, in 2023, and its 2027 problems are all handoffs between systems.

evidence.what: Omnichannel since 2023.
evidence.shows: The company's incidents match the stage's predicted problem.

transition_in.introduces: Where the running example stands.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: The steps, the entities, the status lines and the walk all show the same thing from different sides: an order is never in one place, so its reliability is a property of the messages between systems, not of any system. A merchant that can compare two copies and safely resend a message has the two capabilities every later chapter builds on.
conclusion.so_what: The cheapest architecture document a newcomer can produce is the table of what each system knows at each moment for one real order; it shows where to look before any system is blamed or replaced.

callback.to: The four colleagues who each drew the part of the order their own system holds.
callback.how: The reader can now draw what none of them drew, the path between the boxes: the message that carries each handoff, what it promises and who owns it.

takeaway.content: Follow one real order through every system with a notebook, write down what each system knows at each moment, and take the questions that follow into your first week, a design review or a vendor demo.
